Then those calls would have to be able to process 5x more oil But if we want blocks to always contain <= 10 million oil to limit processing cost Then to avoid those two invariants colliding with each other, calls with > 2 million oil would have to be impossible But there's lots of use cases for meta transactions today that need >2 million gas I think the general case is that if *any* operation costs more in OIL than it goes in GAS than a child execution frame can cause a full revert. right, and if you make an untrusted call, then the untrusted call can cause a full revert Which means meta transactions do not work Because the relayer would have to trust the transactor to not have a buggy transaction that dosses them we mention in the post that taking that it might be possible to calculate a tighter upper bound than the naive one how tight it is going to be, I do not know yet, but this can be checked with relatively simple heuristic so I would not call it dead just yet Basically: 1. We can guarantee blocks will contain <= 10 million oil Is an impossible triangle Any thoughts on exposing the actual gas schedule to the EVM? Something like a `TAILCALL` opcode that does a `CALL` but, it occurs *after* the current call frame is done, and the gas for it is reserved up front. 😆 We considered this in 2014 It was called POST then The only reason we dropped it is because there was not enough time to implement it I see the connection to metatransactions Though it does not resolve the second-to-last poster's concern on that thread, which is that without in-EVM gas checking, there is no way to verify that the meta tx sender's contract is being called with the amount of gas that the meta tx sender expects It doesn't fix the observability/backwards-incompatible problem exactly, but combined with OIL + TAILCALL + GET_GAS_SCHEDULE_FOR .... might make for a sustainable ecosystem where we can change costs, measure different types of limits with different schedules, and preserve metatransactions... <@!273808422753796097> I'm not finding whatever post your mentioning > Though it does not resolve the second-to-last poster's concern on that thread > In the metatx case, the gas limit specified as part of the inner call has actually a more important role : protecting the meta tx signer that its meta-tx is executed with the exact amount specified by its signed message. In other word, the gas limit act here as a lower bound. Else the relayer could maliciously make the inner call fails while getting paid as a result (due to 63/64 rule). > > As EIP-1930 1 points out, such “strict gas semantic for call” is not possible to do it today without relying on tricks (relying on the 63/64 rules) or specific opcode pricing (by computing the amount of gas required to perform the call). See details in EIP-1930. > > None of the proposals here would help. ^ this part Here was my rephrasing: > Basically, the problem is that we are trying to protect against misreporting on both sides. The meta tx signer specifies an amount of gas G that they claim is sufficient to execute their tx. The signer needs an assurance that the tx actually will be executed with G gas, and not less. Meanwhile the relayer needs an assurance that they will actually be spending G gas on the meta tx and not more. > > So the two sides need to negotiate and agree on G, and for that agreement to be enforceable. The current way to enforce G is to have the meta tx signer only approve payment to a specific contract that puts G gas on the sub-call. But all of these proposals make G flexible at origin level and unreadable at contract level, and so they break this approach. Basically, the meta transaction use case seems to inherently require some kind of in-EVM-code gas awareness Anything unobservable like OIL will muck that up on both sides. Assuming any opcode is priced higher in OIL than GAS, then both caller and callee could cause a revert by intentionally burning OIL, so it seems that if preserving metatransactions is a requirement, we have to maintain observability. And breaking metatransactions would probably be really unpopular. Unless we gave users a better way of achieving the same goals.
